title: Study identifies factors that exacerbated the 2024 flash flood in l'Horta Sud
summary: The severity of the flooding experienced by l'Horta Sud on Oct. 29, 2024, can be explained by a combination of exceptional rainfall, near-simultaneous rises in several ravines and a heavily urbanized area, according to a study carried out by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), which reconstructs the event using rainfall data and mathematical models capable of simulating how rain is transformed into runoff, how water carries sediment and how the flood spreads across the territory.

DOI: 10.1016/j.ejrh.2026.103793 The severity of the flooding experienced by l'Horta Sud on Oct. 29, 2024, can be explained by a combination of exceptional rainfall, near-simultaneous rises in several ravines and a heavily urbanized area, according to a study carried out by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), which reconstructs the event using rainfall data and mathematical models capable of simulating how rain is transformed into runoff, how water carries sediment and how the flood spreads across the territory. The study, carried out by Carles Beneyto, Jaime Alberto Cachay-Melly, José Ángel Aranda, Miguel Á. Eguibar, Rafael García-Bartual and Félix Francés, researchers at IIAMA-UPV, has been published in the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies . Coinciding with the second anniversary of the DANA floods on Oct. 29, the study provides a better understanding of what happened and offers lessons to strengthen prevention measures against Mediterranean flash floods. The convergence of the floods multiplied the water inflows One of the main conclusions is that the flood cannot be explained solely by the flow rate of the Poyo ravine. In fact, most of the ravines analyzed reached their peak flows between 6:30 p.m. and 7:50 p.m., causing large quantities of water from different watercourses to converge within a very short time frame, thereby exacerbating the flood. "To understand the scale of the flooding, we need to analyze how the various ravines responded and when their water levels peaked. The convergence of large volumes of water and sediment within a very short time frame was a key factor in exacerbating the scale of the flooding," explains Beneyto, lead author of the study. In this regard, the simulations indicate that the system's combined inflow was approximately 7,000 cubic meters per second before the main overflows. "This figure represents a combined estimate of the inflows from the ravines, not a flow rate measured at a single point," states the IIAMA study. Furthermore, the sequence of rainfall proved decisive, as the morning's rain had already saturated the catchment areas, "which led to a faster and more intense response to the exceptional rainfall in the afternoon," explains Beneyto. Sediment and urban development exacerbated the effects The study estimates that sediments accounted for approximately 7% of the total flood volume, rising to around 19% at peak flow rates. "These materials increased resistance to flow and contributed to reducing the drainage capacity of the watercourses, exacerbating the effects of the flooding," notes Francés, professor of hydraulic engineering and a researcher at IIAMA. Furthermore, development in floodplains, infrastructure and artificial barriers influenced the paths water took and the depths it reached. "The results show that the impacts depended both on the magnitude of the floods and on their interaction with the landscape," states Francés. To reconstruct these processes, the researchers used the TETIS hydrological model, developed at IIAMA, and high-resolution hydraulic simulations. The reconstruction consistently reproduced the general extent of the observed flooding, although it has limitations in representing temporary obstacles and urban details that locally altered water flow. Planning that takes all processes into account In their study, the UPV team warns that episodes of this complexity cannot be assessed solely through statistical estimates of flow rates at specific points. "One of the main lessons is that we must assess rainfall, catchment response, sediment transport and land use together. Integrating these processes is essential for improving risk assessment, spatial planning and preventive measures against extreme flooding in the Mediterranean region," concludes Francés. More information Carles Beneyto et al., Reconstruction of the October 2024 flood in l'Horta Sud (Valencia, Spain), Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies (2026).
